# Summary of Information on Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer who made significant contributions to computer architecture and VLSI design methodology. After early education and gender transition challenges, including being fired from IBM in 1968 for transitioning and later receiving a public apology and lifetime achievement award from IBM in 2020, Conway went on to a distinguished career. She worked on the Advanced Computing Systems project at IBM, notably inventing multiple-issue out-of-order instruction scheduling and contributing to the first superscalar design. At Xerox PARC, she led the LSI Systems group where she co-founded multiproject wafer technology and collaborated with Carver Mead on VLSI design; their book, *Introduction to VLSI Systems* , became a foundational text widely used in chip design education. Conway also innovated scalable and dimensionless chip design rules and created the MOSIS system, an internet-based infrastructure for rapid prototyping and fabrication of chip designs.
Conway held academic positions at MIT and the University of Michigan, contributed to the U.S. Department of Defense Strategic Computing Initiative, and unearthed and publicized her earlier work in the 2000s to break barriers as a transgender pioneer in computer science. She introduced the concept now termed the "Conway effect," describing how marginalized innovators are often overlooked historically. Beyond technical achievements, Conway was an active transgender rights advocate, working to expand understanding, equal opportunity, and protections for transgender individuals, and critiqued controversial typologies in transgender studies. She passed away at age 86 in June 2024, leaving a legacy as a revolutionary technologist, educator, and civil rights activist.
